nameStory: Purple bergamot gets its name from its lavender-purple flowers and its citrusy, bergamot-like fragrance when you crush the leaves. The name "bergamot" comes from the Italian city of Bergamo, famous for citrus oils, though this native mint isn't related to the citrus fruit at all!
description: Purple bergamot is a medium-sized wildflower that grows 2-3 feet tall in wet, swampy areas of eastern North America. Like all members of the mint family, it has square stems and opposite leaves that smell wonderfully minty when crushed. Its tubular reddish-purple flowers cluster together in dense, rounded heads that buzz with visiting bees and butterflies throughout summer.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tubular reddish-purple flowers cluster in dense, rounded heads at the top of stems, with purplish leafy bracts underneath that look like a fancy collar

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Square stems that feel distinctly four-sided when you roll them between your fingers - a telltale sign of the mint family

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Lance-shaped leaves arranged in opposite pairs along the stem, releasing a pleasant minty fragrance when rubbed or crushed

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: After flowering, develops attractive seed heads that goldfinches and other small birds love to visit for the nutritious seeds

habitat: Look for purple bergamot in wet, swampy places like stream banks, marshes, and soggy meadows throughout New England. It thrives in consistently moist to wet soils where many other wildflowers can't survive. You'll often find it growing alongside other water-loving plants like cardinal flower and monkey flower.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge from underground rhizomes (spreading root stems) in late spring, with square stems and opposite mint-scented leaves quickly identifying it as a Monarda.
seasonality.summer: Showy reddish-purple flower clusters bloom from mid to late summer, attracting bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds to wet meadows and stream sides.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade to brown seed heads that birds visit frequently, while leaves may turn yellowish before dying back to ground level.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to underground rhizomes, with no visible parts above ground until spring growth begins again.

funFact: Purple bergamot can actually clone itself underground! It spreads through rhizomes to form large colonies that are essentially one giant plant - so that beautiful patch of purple flowers might actually be a single individual that's been quietly expanding its territory for decades.
confusionNotes: Purple bergamot is easily confused with its more common cousin wild bergamot, but wild bergamot has pinkish-lavender (not reddish-purple) flowers and grows in dry prairies rather than swamps. Remember: purple bergamot loves wet feet, wild bergamot prefers dry ground!
contextualKnowledge: Despite sharing the name "bergamot" with the citrus fruit used to flavor Earl Grey tea, this native wildflower is completely unrelated to citrus. The name connection comes purely from their similar fragrances - early European settlers named it after the familiar scent they recognized from Italian bergamot oranges.
compareHints: Among New England's bergamots, purple bergamot is unique for its wetland habitat and reddish-purple flowers. Wild bergamot has pinker flowers and grows in dry areas, while scarlet beebalm has bright red flowers and also prefers moister spots but isn't as swamp-loving as purple bergamot. The wet habitat is often your best first clue to purple bergamot's identity.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Wild bergamot differs from its flashier cousin scarlet beebalm by its pink-lavender flowers (versus bright red) and its preference for drier soils.
While wild bergamot and scarlet beebalm flaunt bright purple and red flowers respectively, spotted horsemint keeps a lower profile with cream-colored blooms.
Scarlet beebalm is easily distinguished from its cousin wild bergamot by its brilliant red flowers (wild bergamot has pale pink or lavender blooms) and preference for moister soils.
Unlike scarlet beebalm's bright red flowers or wild bergamot's pale pink-purple blooms, lemon beebalm has distinctly tiered purple flower clusters.
